title: Viral Vector Vaccines Strategic Business Research Report 2024-2030 | Expanding Pipeline of Infectious Disease Targets Strengthens the Commercial Outlook - ResearchAndMarkets.com
content: The press release from ResearchAndMarkets.com reports that the global market for viral vector vaccines was valued at US$773.4 million in 2024 and is projected to reach US$893.2 million by 2030, growing at a CAGR of 2.4 % (Business Wire).  The pediatric patient segment is expected to hit US$527.5 million in 2030 with a 1.8 % CAGR, while the adult segment is forecast to grow at 3.4 % CAGR over the same period.  Regionally, the U.S. market is estimated at $210.7 million in 2024 and China is projected to reach $169.9 million by 2030, growing at 4.6 % CAGR (Business Wire).  Key players highlighted include AstraZeneca, Bharat Biotech, CanSino Biologics, Emergent BioSolutions, GlaxoSmithKline, Johnson & Johnson (Janssen), Merck, Oxford Biomedica, Sanofi, and Vaxart, among others (Business Wire).  The report emphasizes that viral vector vaccines—using genetically modified viruses such as adenoviruses, lentiviruses, and vesicular stomatitis virus—offer rapid, scalable, and immunogenic solutions that were pivotal during the COVID‑19 pandemic and are now expanding into oncology and autoimmune indications (Business Wire).  The release notes that increased public and private funding, streamlined regulatory pathways, and growing demand for versatile platforms are driving market expansion (Business Wire).

title: Memo Therapeutics AG Publishes Phase I Safety, Tolerability, and Pharmacokinetics Study for Neutralizing Antibody Targeting BKPyV Infection in Clinical and Translational Science
content: Memo Therapeutics AG has published the results of a Phase I clinical trial for its lead asset, potravitug, a neutralizing antibody targeting BK polyomavirus (BKPyV) infection in kidney transplant recipients. The study demonstrated the safety and tolerability of potravitug in healthy adults, with no serious adverse events reported. The treatment was well tolerated, and a treatment dose of 1000 mg was established for potravitug administered four times with a four-week interval between doses. According to Erik van den Berg, CEO of MTx, 'The positive safety profile and convenient dosing regimen for potravitug demonstrated in this Phase I study establishes a strong basis for the development of potravitug as a first-in-class therapeutic candidate for treating BK polyomavirus infection in kidney transplantation.' Plans are underway to progress potravitug into a Phase III trial, with the potential to transform the treatment landscape for kidney transplant patients with BKPyV infection.

title: Multivalent mpox protein nanoparticle vaccines confer cross-protection against orthopoxvirus infection
content:
The article reports that mpox (MPXV) is a zoonotic disease with symptoms similar to smallpox, including fever, lymphadenopathy, and rash. It cites that since May 2022 there have been 99,176 confirmed cases and 208 deaths across 116 countries, prompting the WHO to declare a Public Health Emergency of International Concern (PHEIC) in July 2022. The PHEIC was lifted after a decline in cases, but a resurgence in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) in 2023 highlighted ongoing challenges. The 2022 epidemic was dominated by the less virulent clade II strain, whereas the more lethal clade I strain—exceeding 10 % mortality—emerged in the DRC in 2023 and spread to neighboring countries by 2024, leading the WHO to declare a second global health emergency. As of 31 December 2024, Africa had 23,489 confirmed cases and the global total reached 12,4753 infected people across 128 countries, underscoring the need for targeted vaccination strategies against clade Ib strains.

MPXV belongs to the orthopoxvirus genus, which includes variola (smallpox) and vaccinia (VACV). Orthopoxviruses share high antigen similarity, enabling cross‑protection; this principle underpinned smallpox eradication via VACV vaccination. No specific antiviral has been approved for mpox, though smallpox‑licensed drugs such as tecovirimat, brincidofovir, and cidofovir have been used off‑label. Current licensed vaccines for MPXV include JYNNEOS (a modified vaccinia Ankara‑based live, non‑replicating vaccine), LC16 (approved for pediatric use), and OrthopoxVac (limited efficacy). JYNNEOS effectiveness against diagnosed mpox in a complete two‑dose regimen was estimated at 66 % during the 2022 outbreaks.

MPXV exists in two infectious forms: the intracellular mature virion (IMV) and the extracellular enveloped virion (EEV). IMV surface antigens (A29, E8, H3) and the assembly/entry protein M1 facilitate cell attachment, while EEV antigens (A35, B6) mediate viral transmission. Studies in animals show that combining antibodies to multiple IMV and EEV antigens enhances protection. Nanoparticle vaccine platforms can present multiple antigens simultaneously, improving immune responses by targeting antigen‑presenting cells.

The authors describe a multivalent nanoparticle vaccine that uses a 60‑mer lumazine synthase (LuS) protein covalently linked to IMV and EEV antigens via a SpyTag/SpyCatcher system. Compared to monovalent formulations, the multivalent nanoparticles induced higher immunogenicity and provided better cross‑protection against a genetically related VACV challenge in mice. A trivalent formulation containing IMV proteins M1 and E8 plus EEV protein B6 elicited robust immunogenicity and significant cross‑protection against VACV in mice, offering a promising approach for future mpox vaccine development.

title: Erasmus MC ontwerpt 'universeel' vogelgriepvaccin dat beschermt tegen meerdere varianten
content: Researchers at Erasmus MC in Rotterdam have developed a 'universal' bird flu vaccine capable of protecting against multiple variants, unlike existing vaccines that target only one strain. The vaccine was tested on ferrets and published in Nature on October 15, 2025. The breakthrough was achieved using a complex technique called antigen cartography, which created a 3D digital model of all known H5 bird flu variants, visualized like a solar system with a central core and surrounding variants. The vaccine targets the central, conserved region of the virus, providing immunity against diverse, distant variants. In tests, vaccinated ferrets showed strong immune responses and were protected from two highly different bird flu subtypes, with no viral replication in the respiratory tract. Experts warn that bird flu is a real pandemic candidate: it has mutated over 30 years to infect various mammals, including foxes, grizzly bears, seals, and dairy cows in the U.S., and has caused nearly 1,000 human infections since 2003, with a 50% fatality rate. While human-to-human transmission remains limited, the virus requires only a few mutations to become pandemic, some of which are already present. Current WHO-regulated strategies rely on developing new vaccines for each emerging variant, but by the time they are deployed, the virus has often mutated further. The Erasmus MC vaccine offers a long-term solution by preparing the immune system for broad protection. The team, led by molecular virologist Mathilde Richard, explains that unlike SARS-CoV-2, bird flu does not trigger herd immunity because of high mortality and isolated animal populations, leading to repeated re-emergence of similar variants globally. The vaccine is intended as a preventive tool during pandemic outbreaks, to be followed by a strain-specific booster. A human safety trial began in summer 2025.

title: Tüm virüslere karşı etkili ilaç geliştirildi: Evrensel bağışıklık mümkün mü?
content: Researchers at Columbia University in the US have developed a universal vaccine that can protect against almost all viruses. The vaccine combines a rare genetic mutation with mRNA technology. The mutation, known as ISG15, was first discovered in 2018 and was found to weaken the body's defenses against bacteria. However, it was found to provide a complete immune response against viruses. The vaccine is administered as a nasal spray and has been shown to provide temporary protection against a wide range of viruses, including the flu, measles, and COVID-19. The treatment activates proteins that fight viruses, but the amount of these proteins is not yet sufficient to make the treatment effective in humans. Researchers are now aiming to produce a protective spray that can combat unknown viruses, potentially preventing future pandemics. Meanwhile, researchers in the UK are using flatworms instead of lab mice in their experiments. They have found that the worms respond similarly to lab mice when given a common antipsychotic medication, 'haloperidol.' This could potentially reduce the number of lab animals used in research, particularly in the field of neuroscience, where lab mice are used in 20-50% of experiments.

title: MNEXSPIKE: Uses, Dosage, Side Effects, Warnings - Drugs.com
content:
The article describes mNEXSPIKE, a COVID‑19 vaccine developed by Moderna that uses mRNA technology to encode the SARS‑CoV‑2 spike protein. It is a 0.2 mL suspension for intramuscular injection and was FDA‑approved on 30 May 2025. The vaccine is intended for adults 65 years and older and for adolescents and adults 12‑64 years who have high‑risk conditions such as chronic respiratory disease, heart disease, diabetes, chronic kidney or liver disease, immunocompromised status, obesity (BMI ≥ 30), cancer history, neurologic conditions, or pregnancy. The article notes that breakthrough infections can still occur but vaccination reduces the risk of severe disease, hospitalization, and death.

mNEXSPIKE works by delivering mRNA that instructs cells to produce the spike protein, triggering an immune response that includes antibody production and memory cell formation. The article lists common side effects—pain, tenderness, swelling, redness at the injection site, fatigue, headache, muscle and joint pain, chills, nausea, vomiting, and fever—which are typically mild to moderate and resolve within 1‑3 days. Serious side effects are rare; the article highlights anaphylaxis and myocarditis/pericarditis. It cites a risk of myocarditis of approximately 27 cases per million doses in males 12‑24 years and about 8 cases per million doses in the general population aged 6 months‑64 years, with symptoms usually beginning within a week of vaccination.

Absolute contraindications include a severe allergy to any previous dose of mNEXSPIKE, SPIKEVAX, or any Moderna COVID‑19 vaccine, or to any vaccine ingredient. The article advises patients with moderate to severe illness or infection to wait until recovery before vaccination. Pregnancy and breastfeeding are considered safe; the vaccine is recommended during pregnancy because COVID‑19 poses serious risks and mRNA vaccines have shown good safety profiles, potentially providing neonatal protection via maternal antibodies.

Administration requires a single 0.2 mL intramuscular dose in the deltoid muscle, with a 15‑30 minute observation period for allergic reactions. The vaccine must be stored at –25 °C to –15 °C for long‑term use, 2 °C to 8 °C for up to 30 days, or at room temperature for up to 24 hours before use. The article lists the active ingredient (mRNA encoding the spike protein) and inactive ingredients (lipids such as SM‑102, PEG 2000 DMG, cholesterol, DSPC, tromethamine, sucrose) and notes that it contains no preservatives, live virus, eggs, gelatin, latex, gluten, antibiotics, or metals.

The article encourages reporting side effects to VAERS and provides contact information. It also advises patients to inform healthcare providers of all medications, especially immunosuppressants or blood thinners, as these can affect vaccine effectiveness or increase bruising risk. The manufacturer is Moderna US, Inc., Princeton, NJ 08540.

Overall, the article presents factual information about the vaccine’s composition, approval, target populations, mechanism, side‑effect profile, contraindications, and storage requirements, with no editorial commentary or bias.

title: Knowledge of viruses can help prevent them
content: The article explains how knowledge of viruses and their vaccines can reduce disease. It notes that viruses are tiny, up to 2000 times smaller than a grain of sand, and carry DNA or RNA inside a capsid that hijacks host cells to replicate. Hepatitis B is highlighted as a common liver infection; five hepatitis viruses (A, B, C, D, E) cause liver inflammation, with A, B, and C being most prevalent and linked to serious illness and cancer. The article states that the hepatitis B vaccine is 95 percent effective in children and adults, is administered within 24 hours of birth followed by doses at 1–2 months and 6–18 months, and that vaccinated individuals are immune for life. It reports that babies infected with hepatitis B have a 90 percent chance of developing chronic disease and that 25 percent of those chronic cases die. The piece also mentions at least seven virus groups that can cause cancer and notes the existence of an HPV vaccine. High‑risk groups include children under 5, adults over 65, people with asthma, diabetes, COPD, weakened immune systems, or who are pregnant. The article concludes that informed decisions about vaccines can promote long, healthy lives and cites the American Academy of Pediatrics as a reliable resource.

title: One-shot vaccines for HIV and covid
content: Researchers treated mice with a dual‑adjuvant vaccine that combines two immune‑stimulating compounds, one of which incorporates a compound previously developed by Scripps professor Darrell Irvine. Irvine and MIT professor J. Christopher Love, the senior authors of the study, found that the combination produced more robust immune responses. In the new paper, they showed that the dual‑adjuvant vaccine accumulated in the lymph nodes, where B cells encounter antigens and undergo rapid mutations that generate new antibodies. The vaccine’s antigens remained in the lymph nodes for up to a month, allowing the immune system to build a greater number and diversity of antibodies against the HIV protein than a vaccine given alone or with a single adjuvant. Love says, 'When you think about the immune system sampling all of the possible solutions, the more chances we give it to identify an effective solution, the better.' The approach may mimic what occurs during a natural infection and could lead to an immune response so strong and broad that vaccines only need to be given once. Love adds, 'It offers the opportunity to engineer new formulations for these types of vaccines across a wide range of different diseases, such as influenza, SARS‑CoV‑2, or other pandemic outbreaks.'

title: Какие вакцины применяют для профилактики ветряной оспы
content: In Russia, cases of chickenpox have rapidly increased since the beginning of 2025, with nearly all regions reporting infections, according to Rospotrebnadzor. Experts attribute this surge to a shortage of vaccines, as no domestic production exists yet, and development of a Russian-made vaccine is only in its early stages. Chickenpox, caused by the Varicella Zoster virus (herpesvirus type 3), spreads via airborne droplets and typically presents with itchy skin rashes, fever, and general malaise. The incubation period lasts about three weeks, and individuals are contagious one to two days before rash onset and remain so for up to five days after the last blister appears. While usually mild in children, severe cases can occur, and the virus remains dormant in the body for life, potentially reactivating later as shingles. Currently, two main vaccines are used in Russia: 'Varilrix' (Belgian) and 'Okavax' (Japanese), both live attenuated vaccines effective from nine months of age. 'Varilrix' may cause allergic reactions, while 'Okavax' induces lasting immunity in 90% of recipients. A combined vaccine, 'Priorix Tetra', protects against measles, mumps, rubella, and chickenpox but faces supply issues. Due to reduced foreign suppliers, vaccine availability has declined, even in private clinics. Despite this, Roszdravnadzor confirmed that chickenpox vaccines remain in stable circulation. Vaccination is not in the national immunization schedule but is included in the regional epidemic indication schedule, with regional authorities deciding on implementation. The vaccination process requires a medical examination, and the injection is administered subcutaneously or intramuscularly. Post-vaccination, patients are advised to avoid strenuous activity and saunas for a few days. A domestically developed vaccine, being co-developed by Russian company 'Nanolek' and South Korean GC Biopharma, is expected to enter production between 2026 and 2027, targeting children from nine months to 17 years. Full registration will require several years of clinical trials. This initiative aims to reduce dependence on foreign imports and improve domestic vaccine accessibility. Earlier reports indicated a rise in Coxsackie virus infections in Russia.

title: Antiviral PPE For The Next Pandemic
content: Scientists have isolated a rare immune mutation, ISG15 immunodeficiency, which grants immunity to known viruses but makes people more susceptible to certain bacterial illnesses. Researchers have found a way to stimulate the production of 10 beneficial proteins created by the mutation using mRNA sequences inside a lipid nanoparticle. Lead researcher Vagelos Bogunovic says, 'we have yet to find a virus that can break through the therapy's defenses.' The treatment, which could be used as biological Personal Protective Equipment (PPE), aims to protect first responders from unknown viruses before new vaccines can be developed. Researchers have successfully tested the treatment in hamsters and mice via nasal drip, and are considering intranasal vaccines for human trials.
